text: With default options (MSE-optimal bandwidth, triangular kernel, local-linear fit, NN variance) rdrobust reports a conventional point estimate of 7.416 (SE 1.4604) for the effect of a Democratic Senate win on the Democratic vote share six years later.
The robust bias-corrected 95% confidence interval for the same default specification is [4.09441, 10.9255]; the article does not print the bias-corrected point estimate.
Setting bandwidths manually to 16.79369 and 27.43745 reproduces the earlier rdrobust (2014) results: conventional estimate 7.4253 and robust interval [4.06975, 10.9833].

Robust bias-corrected tests of the RD effect on four predetermined covariates (class, termshouse, termssenate, population) give p-values 0.897, 0.561, 0.901 and 0.634, so none rejects balance at the cutoff.
A McCrary density test of the running variable around the cutoff gives p = 0.39 in the Senate data, with no evidence of sorting.

In the selected window [-0.75, 0.75], chosen by balance tests on eight predetermined covariates at alpha 0.15, the randomization-based difference in means is 9.32 with 95% CI [4.60, 14.78] (22 treated, 15 control).
The conventional nonparametric local-linear estimate with the 2014 rdrobust bandwidth (16.79) is 7.43 with robust interval [4.07, 10.98], and the 4th-order parametric fit gives 9.41.
The Senate data contain 1,390 elections from 1914 to 2010 with running variable the Democratic margin of victory at t and outcome the Democratic vote share at t+2.
The rdlocrand package implements randomization-based RD inference under local randomization, and its Senate illustration uses the same Cattaneo, Frandsen and Titiunik (2015) data and covariates.
In U.S. House elections from 1942 to 2008, bare winners and bare losers differ markedly on pretreatment covariates, and covariate imbalance worsens in the closest races.

Eggers et al. (2015) find that the pattern of incumbent parties winning very close House races does not appear in other electoral settings and conclude that the RD assumptions are likely to hold in a wide variety of electoral settings. This claim rests on the abstract only.
